newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Antarctic summit moves to prevent penguin infections.
newsitem.headline: Antarctic summit moves to prevent penguin infections.

text.p: Tougher environmental restrictions are being prepared to prevent Antarctic penguins from getting infections passed on by humans, a New Zealand Antarctic spokesman said on Thursday.

Stuart Prior, head of the New Zealand delegation at the 21st Antarctic Treaty meeting in Christchurch, said on Wednesday there had always been fears that the growing number of people in Antarctica would eventually infect penguins.
These have been confirmed by Australian scientists who have found emperor penguins infected by a poultry virus, probably introduced by humans.
"However, the Antarctic environment protocol, soon to be ratified, should reduce the risk of any further infections being transmitted in future," Prior told reporters.
"It's highly likely that someone may have unwittingly thrown away chicken remains, birds have eaten it and it has been passed on to penguins."
There is no poultry at the Antarctic bases and the poultry infection could have been passed on from tourists.
Prior said it was important that tourists who visit the penguin colonies have clean clothing and boots before stepping on the ice.
The Antarctic penguins have been relatively disease-free until now, with their remoteness helping them avoid viruses common to other birds.
But Australian scientists have found both adelie and emperor penguins in the Ross Sea area with infections common to domestic chickens.

Rex Moncur, director of the Australian Antarctic division and who presented a paper on penguin infections to the 43-nation meeting, said the poultry virus causes serious disease in chicks, increases their susceptibility to other infections and reduces growth rates.
"These subtle effects can impact on the long-term survival of a species. It may also cause high rates of death among chicks," he said in his address to the meeting.
"The movement of people from one bird (or seal) colony to another also increases the risk of spreading naturally occurring endemic diseases."
Moncur said there was a need to develop measures to limit the threat and to control outbreaks.
The impact of the virus on the penguins could lead to local extinction of the species.
